title: Learn About AI Sustainability in a Free Online Course
content:
The new "Sustainability and AI" online course explores different dimensions of AI sustainability. The course consists of four video lectures, accompanied by an optional assignment. The lectures are delivered by Sara Pyykölä, a doctoral researcher at the University of Helsinki.

During the course, you will learn, for example: 

  • What sustainable AI and the sustainable use of AI mean 
  • What AI requires to function and what influences its environmental footprint 
  • How AI works from a technical perspective 
  • How to apply the knowledge gained to your own work 

    • The course provides information on the sustainability of AI for anyone interested in the topic. It is particularly aimed at entrepreneurs. The course has been developed as part of the GENGREEN project, which supports the sustainable business skills of SMEs and especially women entrepreneurs through education and Nordic networking. The project is funded by the Interreg Aurora Programme of the European Union.

title: Kimalaiset ratkaisevat ongelmia kuin kädelliset – uusi tutkimus haastaa käsityksiä eläinten älykkyydestä
content:
More than 100 years ago, psychologist Wolfgang Köhler famously showed that chimpanzees could solve novel problems by suddenly combining objects in new ways, such as stacking boxes to reach an out-of-reach banana. These experiments became some of the earliest and most influential demonstrations of insight and spontaneous problem-solving in animals.

Now, researchers from the University of Oulu, the University of Helsinki, and the University of Turku report strikingly similar problem-solving abilities in bumble bees.

In a new study published in Science, bumble bees (Bombus terrestris) solved a completely novel object-manipulation task without being trained on the solution itself. The bees first learned that a blue artificial flower signalled reward. During the test, the flower was moved to the ceiling of a transparent arena, out of reach. To access it, the bees had to spontaneously generate a novel solution by moving a ball underneath the flower and climbing onto it, a behavioural sequence they had never previously encountered or been trained to perform.

title: Koekäyttö: Prensa Libre Digital Archive 11.9. asti
content:
Founded in 1951, Prensa Libre is a leading newspaper published in Guatemala City and distributed nationwide. The newspaper was conceived with the purpose of maintaining an independent voice, to provide impartial reporting on local news and bringing to light transgressions of government and public figures. Prensa Libre has covered critical moments in Guatemalan and Latin American history, including political upheaval, assassinations, and coups; peace treaties and elections; natural disasters; economic and technological developments; and Guatemalans on the international stage;

title: Helsingin yliopiston sijoitustuotto puoli miljardia euroa vuodesta 2019
content:
The University of Helsinki’s financial investments’ return was 9.8 percent from January to June 2026, which increased the investments’ value to EUR 914 million. The investments have returned 138.2 percent or approximately EUR 500 million since 2019, when the university adopted the current investment strategy. The compound annual return (CAGR) has been 12.3 percent per annum, which is roughly two percentage points more than the 10.4 percent for the benchmark index.

“Predicting stock markets’ short-term movements has scientifically been found to be so challenging, that it generally does not pay off – despite its superficial attractiveness. We would not have obtained these returns and would now have a significantly lower capacity to carry risk, if we would have acted on the recurring warnings of weak expected returns”, Chief Investment Officer Anders Ekholm summarizes.

“In the long run, companies’ business operations drive stock returns, and we can expect a premium for the risk. We must take care of our risk management, so that we are able to continue investing in the long run under all circumstances, also during strong turbulence”, Chief Financial Officer Marjo Berglund continues.

title: Unipöksyt paljastavat: Vauvojen yöheräämiset yleisempiä kuin vanhemmat luulevat
content:
Almost half of Finnish parents feel that their infants’ sleep is abnormal. However, measuring sleep disturbances is complicated.

In her doctoral thesis, University of Helsinki researcher Sofie de Sena investigated infant sleep using a smart wearable system called NAPPA (NAPping PAnts). It measures infant sleep at home and provides information on body position, respiration and activity.

“This is a substantial leap forward in assessing infant sleep. The smart wearable system monitors the child without interruption, making it possible to monitor sleep without disturbing day-to-day life,” says de Sena.

De Sena compared parental assessments of children’s sleep with results obtained from the NAPPA wearables.

“Parents miss brief awakenings altogether, and they overestimate the duration of longer ones. It is important to distinguish between parental estimates of children’s sleep and how they actually sleep. Direct measurement is the only route to objective understanding of infant sleep,” de Sena points out.

title: “Ilman pölyttäjiä maailma olisi ankea ja väritön” – Uusi näyttely avaa oven pölyttäjien kiehtovaan elämään
content:
Pollinators represent an astonishingly diverse group of animals, many of which possess remarkable abilities despite their small size. Bees can count, bumblebees solve problems, and on distant islands, even lizards can pollinate flowers.

The  exhibition, which combines science and art, offers a wealth of information, stunning visuals, and fun activities for visitors of all ages. Guests can play interactive games like "Identify the Pollinators" and "Pollinator Protection Bingo," design their own imaginary pollinator, and explore the museum's impressive collection of specimens. The exhibition is based on a newly illustrated non-fiction book.

– We want to show the world through the eyes of pollinators, says exhibition scriptwriter Mia Rönkä, Adjunct Professor in Environmental Ecology at the University of Turku. Rönkä has written the exhibition’s informational texts and poems.

Although the sensory perceptions, cognitive abilities, and communication methods of pollinators like bees differ from ours as humans, we can still strive to understand and appreciate them as individuals of other species – without anthropomorphizing them, Rönkä explains.

title: Arkadiankadun siltaremontti aiheuttaa muutoksia liikennejärjestelyihin Luonnontieteellisen museon lähistöllä
content:
The renovation will start with the construction of temporary traffic arrangements from Wednesday 7 January onwards. The renovation is expected to be completed in late 2026.

A temporary bridge for pedestrians will be built on the east side of Arkadiankatu over the Baana. The aim is to maintain the pedestrian route on the east side of the bridge until the temporary bridge is operational. Cyclists will also be able to use the bridge.

The Baana route underneath the bridge is expected to remain open for most of the renovation's duration, with some minor exceptions.

There will be changes to the motor vehicle routes by the bridge and around it in January. If possible, should be favoured during the bridge renovation.

Connections to the bus terminals in Kamppi will remain available, but there will be a slight diversion of routes.

Trams 1 and 1T will run via Simonkatu and Kamppi. Lasipalatsi and the Natural History Museum will not be served.

The diversion is due to the renovation of the Arkadiankatu bridge and will remain in place until late 2026. The renovation will not affect HSL's bus services.

title: Ukrainan sota - yliopiston suositukset
content:
The University of Helsinki has condemned the military action by Russia and expressed its support for Ukraine and its university community. We have also expressed our support for Ukraine, together with other Finnish universities, through statements by and the . As a demonstration of support, we have illuminated buildings in the colours of the Ukrainian flag and raised the flag on our premises.

One of the principles of the University of Helsinki is to promote international collaboration in research and higher education, and to support these efforts even in difficult circumstances. Russia’s indefensible military aggression in Ukraine has required exceptional measures, which include those taken in the collaboration between universities.

The University of Helsinki is monitoring both national and EU-level sanctions, adapting our policies and processes accordingly. Together with other Finnish and international universities, the University of Helsinki strives to promote the end of military action in Ukraine, while supporting Ukrainian institutions and people.

title: European Declaration on Heat and Health
content:
June 2026 was the hottest June ever recorded in Western Europe. Several thousand excess deaths were registered in the peak heatwave week alone, and the toll is still rising — alongside wildfires and crop losses across the continent.

And yet this is not a failure of planning. Most European countries have heat-health action plans and early warning systems. The EU adopted an Adaptation Strategy in 2021 and declared a climate emergency back in 2019.
We know the danger. Too little is happening.

The European Commission is now preparing the European Climate Resilience Framework, due for adoption at the end of 2026. It will decide whether this summer finally leads to binding obligations — or to another strategy without consequence.

That is why HELSUS has joined the European Regional Hub of the Planetary Health Alliance and more than 80 organisations in the European Declaration on Heat and Health, calling on the EU to put health at the centre of its climate policy: with legally binding adaptation obligations, measurable health targets, and a European Heat-Health Action Plan with an emergency fund for hospitals, care homes, nurseries and schools.

title: A short training program co-organizer for visitors from China
content:
HELSUS and co-organized a one-week training program on sustainability science for 34 visiting students from seven different HEIs of the Jiangsu province, China on 3–7 August 2026. Most of these 2nd and 3rd year university students came from Nanjing (Agricultural University; Forestry University; and University of Information Science and Technology) and the others from Hohai, Jiangnan, Yangzhou, and Jiangsu Universities. The week of sustainability training in Helsinki was the first part of a three-week visiting program Smart Agriculture Frontiers – Modern Agriculture and Sustainable Development organized in collaboration with JAMK University of Applied Science.

Each day focused on a different theme of global sustainability providing the group of students from diverse disciplinary backgrounds with an overview of research and education at the University of Helsinki. The lectures given by HELSUS researchers and other colleagues on Kumpula and Viikki campuses addressed the importance of interdisciplinary research in innovations in bioeconomy, solutions for energy transition, and life cycle assessment, as well as insights on research on global environmental change and climate change. The final day of the first week ended with lectures on the global food systems, including food production and the environment, and circular food systems.

We also organized our Chinese guests a guided tour on the Viikki Research Farm to learn about its role in the production of scientific data and knowledge for solving sustainability challenges in agriculture. They also visited the Nihtisilta Recycling Centre to experience circular economy in practice. In addition, the group travelled to the Lammi Biological Station to get to know about its research, education and societal impact, and of course, to experience the Finnish nature.

title: Professori Kai Puolamäki tutkii tekoälyn sisuksia
content:
Professor of Computer Science Kai Puolamäki uses AI to investigate new ways of modelling atmospheric particles. His research focuses on how to make machine learning models understandable, how to assess their uncertainties and how researchers can use them to discover new knowledge.

You have likely used AI, whether in your free time or at work. But do you really know how it works? There is no need to feel embarrassed if you don’t.

“No one fully understands how complex, self-learning AI models actually work,” says Professor of Computer Science and Athmospheric Sciences of the University of Helsinki.

“The software involved is so extensive and complex that even the people who develop it don’t know everything about it.”

Even so, Puolamäki is working to uncover what is happening inside these models for a very practical reason.

“Picture a study where AI analyses data on the researcher’s behalf. If the researcher doesn’t understand what’s happening, it’s difficult for them to judge how reliable the AI’s conclusions are.”

This is why we must understand AI better to use it effectively.
